title: Culture is driven by evolution
subtitle: Biology's false binary
author: Ruth Mace
introduction: The debate over whether it is evolution or culture that shapes human behaviour is one of the biggest in modern science. Yet, amidst these discussions, a more nuanced perspective emerges: there is no division between ‘evolution’ and ‘culture’ – culture itself is part of our evolutionary story, argues Ruth Mace.
body:
This article is presented in association with Closer To Truth, an esteemed partner for the 2024 HowTheLightGetsIn Festival.

This question is taboo in university anthropology departments; many of them dissolved into acrimony debating if culture or evolution drives human behaviour.  Some universities decided to split their anthropology departments, with social or cultural anthropology in one building, and evolutionary anthropologists elsewhere.  In my own department, we agree to differ (although from time to time I learn that someone has not spoken to me for 30 years because of my being in the ‘bad’ camp).  Fortunately, most of our students are now leaving that particular culture war behind.

Evolution designs not just our bodies but also our minds

We are evolved beings.  If you want to understand the design of living things, then there are only two options – evolution by natural selection, or divine creation.  If you are happy with divine creation, then I assume that makes it pretty uncomplicated. If not, you are left with evolution.  Evolution designs not just our bodies but also our minds.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Biology beyond genes With Denis Noble

We are also cultural beings.  We are incredibly diverse in terms of how we behave, depending at least in part on where we grew up.  The rules and norms that both govern and divide us, differ from place to place, from one cultural group to another, and are familiar to us from childhood.  These rules reach into every corner of our lives: how we marry, how often we reproduce, how we speak, how we treat males and females and other genders, what we eat, and what we believe.

Natural selection ensures that genes are great at designing your behaviour so that you and your kin survive and reproduce as successfully as possible.  An animal’s instincts can guide them through eating and mating, or even making complex structures like weaver birds’ nests.  If you are a kittiwake, your instincts even make sure you don’t jump about too much when you are a chick, because otherwise you will fall off the cliff ledge on which your parents are raising you.  Some more elaborate behaviours might require more learning to perfect.  The weaver birds do apparently get better at nest building with experience.  But trial and error is a slow and costly process.

Humans use trial and error too, but we have another trick.  We are masters of cultural learning.  We learn from each other, often in very specific detail. Whilst the chimpanzee is struggling through all the options trying to figure out what it might be able to use to crack a nut, you are reaching for a nutcracker in your kitchen drawer.  You might work out how to use it all by yourself, but almost certainly have no idea how to smelt the metal to make the nutcracker.  You don’t need to know, as you are benefiting from the trial and error, intuition and innovation of multiple generations of long dead metalworkers, who learnt from each other.  For a small price, you can buy yourself a tool that was created by thousands of years of cumulative effort, so you don’t need to learn how to make it.  Even if you think you could make a nutcracker, you almost certainly could not make your smartphone or your car.

Animals use cultural learning too, but not to the same degree as humans.  We are desperate to learn.  Children are sponges and especially quick at learning languages.  It is language that fuels our cultural ability.  Our big brains and linguistic abilities are outliers on the primate lineage.  We also have long lives and live in loosely connected, mobile groups, which makes conditions ideal for the transmission of cultural traits.

In the first half of the twentieth century, animal behaviourists were obsessed with how much of behaviour can be attributed to ‘nature’ versus ‘nurture’.  The question soon spilt over into discourse about human behaviour and psychology. But calculating how much of each is in play turns out to be a complicated task.  The answer very much depends on how much environmental variation there is.  But more importantly, it turned out not to be a very productive academic pathway.  The answer is always: it is both.   A much more fruitful question is to ask how did evolution design that behaviour?  Why do we do that, in the sense of why did evolution select for that?

It is our greatest instinct to be cultural

Other species are bad at building on prior knowledge.  Technological innovation is one of our superpowers, that has driven our success as a species.  Our ancestors made simple technological advances, and the next generation elaborated it, and that process repeats again and again. We have used technology to live everywhere, to hunt anything, to exploit just about any resource and to massively increase the human population (wiping out many other hominid species in the process). It is no surprise that a brain exceptionally capable of cultural learning might do well in terms of biological fitness.

It is our greatest instinct to be cultural.  We don’t like to be the odd one out, preferring to behave in line with our community, on whose good opinion we depend heavily.  If we face a problem we do not know how to solve, we tend to follow what we think most other people are doing. Cultural norms teach us how to navigate our physical and social environment.  They can make life somewhat constrained, especially in close-knit societies where traditions are strong, but such a way of life is also less fraught with constant decision-making.

Useful as they are, cultural norms may not always feel like friends.  There may be occasions when what we want to do, and what society wants us to do, are not the same.   Behavioural dilemmas normally arise when our instinct is to be selfish (to protect ourselves or our family, to make a personal gain at the expense of others, even to eat too much), when norms might dictate that we should share (food or wealth), or fight for the common good (literally in a war, or in other ways, like working on a communal project or obeying the law).  Natural selection is very good at selecting for the former, but not the latter; selecting ‘for the good of the group’ is not the way evolution works. Natural selection overwhelmingly prioritises the benefits of the individual and their descendants. There are numerous occasions where group and individual benefits do align, which is why we are such social beings. We evolved to live and even breed communally, relying on each others help to feed and protect ourselves and our children.  Being nasty and selfish is never a good look and won’t get you far in such an environment.  But if individual or family benefits do not align with the good of the wider group, coercion or punishment may be the only force that is maintaining a group-beneficial behaviour.

SUGGESTED READING A new theory of matter may help explain life By Lee Cronin

Inequalities in power make punishment easier.  Powerful leaders can make rules that force us to do uncomfortable things (for example fight in war); but we may accept their authority, to make us behave in costly ways, if the leaders in turn provide us with a useful good (like preventing our society from being overrun and slaughtered by an enemy).   We prefer to live under the rule of law rather than face the dangers of living in anarchy.  That said, if possibilities arise to behave selfishly without being spotted by others, then cheating will abound.  Punishment can take the form of malicious gossip and ostracism – we talk badly of those caught doing self-serving things, even if we ourselves might be tempted to do the same in the privacy of our own lives.

You are going to have hard time working out what is a biological instinct, and what is a cultural norm

Inequalities are not just between leaders and followers.  They can be between the sexes, or even between parents and offspring.  Such evolutionary conflicts of interest may not necessarily result in actual fights; if it is simply less costly to learn that you cannot win, you may do better to accept an unequal share of whatever is at stake.  Often people appear to happily accept norms that are unfair.  One sex may be more powerful, making the cost of resistance too great for the weaker sex.  Obeying your parents, perhaps doing something that favours them or your siblings, rather than yourself, may be trained into you from a young age. Accepting inequality may be less costly than constantly fighting a losing battle - and you may not even be aware you are doing it.

In short, you are going to have hard time working out what is a biological instinct, and what is a cultural norm.  If you move to live in a new culture, you will no doubt find yourself constantly being told off, or worse, for ‘doing the wrong thing’.  Following the wrong cultural norm is costly; so a capacity for culture is clearly a useful trait that will feel instinctual.   So good luck sorting out if your motives derive from culture or biology – it is probably the wrong question to ask.
